title: Bartlett updates two centuries of chairmen, JPR burns the candle at both ends, in political notes
summary: The House Judiciary Committee changes more than 200 years of history with new chair, Del. J. Sandy Bartlett, and the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee wastes no time getting into the nitty-gritty of bill hearings, in political notes.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 16, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 16, 2026

The Department of Legislative Services is the keeper of all legislative arcana, among other things. So it was able to respond relatively quickly this week to a request for information about House Judiciary Committee leadership, spitting out a list of chairs — or, more strictly, chairmen — dating back to 1828.

They might want to put an asterisk next to this year’s entry.

Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), recently elevated from vice chair of Judiciary, is not just the first woman to make that 198-year list of committee chairs, she is also the first person of color to chair the committee. She was appointed by new House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), who made former Judiciary Chair Del. Luke Clippinger (D-Baltimore City) her speaker pro tem.

Del. Debra Davis (D-Charles) was named vice chair, making the Judiciary Committee the only standing committee this year chaired by two Black women.

“We have quite a team. We have the dream team here, I hope. I think we do,” Bartlett said during an organizational hearing for the committee this week.

“We do,” Davis replied.

In an interview Friday, Bartlett said she was grateful for the chance to serve as chair, which she said comes with a “strong sense of responsibility.” She said she thinks about her ancestors when serving in the legislature, including her great-grandfather Bryant William Thorpe, one of four Black state legislators in North Carolina in 1885.

Peña-Melnyk unveils House leadership shake-up, expands standing committees

“I am just so grateful. It hasn’t even really completely hit me yet because I stand on the shoulders of other people, but I know it’s special,” Bartlett said. “I know it’s historic, and I appreciate it.”

It’s not the first committee to be led by two Black women: Last year, the House Ways and Means Committee was chaired by Del. Vanessa Atterbeary (D-Howard) and the vice chair was Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery). When Atterbeary stepped down this year to focus on her race for Howard County executive, Wilkins was made chair. Her vice chair is Del. Jessica Feldmark (D-Howard).

The only other standing committee led by two Black legislators is Senate Executive Nominations chaired by Sen. Benjamins Brooks (D-Baltimore County) and Sen. C. Anthony Muse (D-Prince George’s) as the vice chair.

The Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee got its nickname, “JPR after dark,” for its habit of holding hearings well into the night to handle its significant workload during previous legislative sessions.

Now, it appears the committee has started burning the candle at both ends.

Committee Manager Sandy Popp informed the committee during an organizational meeting Thursday that the committee had already scheduled 58 prefiled bills to be heard this month, a little more than a fifth of the 273 bills that had been submitted to the full Senate as of Friday. Popp said that’s down from the 75 prefiled bills the committee started with last year.

Hearings will begin Tuesday and be packed in over the next 10 days. (The Senate Education, Energy and the Environment Committee is keeping pace with 65 bill hearings scheduled, but those start Wednesday and are currently scheduled through mid-February.)

“The work that we do here is, I think, most directly connected to how people move about their everyday lives, and you’ll see that through testimony,” said Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), chair of the committee.

And the committee has not packed the calendar with softball bills. About 31 bills will be reviewed next week on topics that include estates and trusts, family law and criminal law. But there is also a potentially a high-octane hearing Thursday when the committee hears Senate Bill 1, prohibiting face coverings for law enforcement officers in the state, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers; and SB 245, prohibiting a county sheriff, local police or any “agent of the state” from entering into an agreement with the federal government to enforce civil immigration law.

Put simply, SB 245 would ban 287(g) agreements with ICE. That language was stripped out of larger bill on the last day of the 2025 session, original sponsor Sen. Karen Lewis Young (D-Frederick) reintroduced it this year with two heavyweight co-sponsors: Smith, the committee chair, and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City).

SB 1, sponsored by Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s),follows months of aggressive immigration raids by ICE agents who are typically masked. The scrutiny intensified after Renee Good, 37, was shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis this month. Augustine’s bill would prohibit officers from wearing items such as a balaclava, ski mask or neck gaiter on duty. It wouldn’t apply to an individual “actively engaged in an undercover operation.”

Ferguson and Pena-Melnyk have both expressed support for the measure.

“I think all of us can sit back and imagine if you’re sitting in your car and somebody runs up to you, even as a law enforcement agent that quickly shows us a badge and has their face covered, I know I would be terrified,” Ferguson said Wednesday to reporter. “It’s just not how you build trust in policing.”

But Sen. William G. Folden (R-Frederick), a Judicial Proceedings member who recently retired from the Frederick Police Department, said law enforcement officers in the state usually do not wear face coverings unless it’s due to inclement weather. He said masked federal officers “are trying to actually find a way to protect themselves and their families from being doxed by certain activists who make it their mission to cause disruption … in the performance of their duties.”

“I find it interesting that the state of Maryland wants to legislate a policy for federal law enforcement officers,” Folden said.

Bartlett could not say when the House version of the masking bill, sponsored by Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s), might be heard in the Judiciary Committee.
